note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: 1 <= k <= n and n mod k = 0
clarifyingQuestions: Must every division be equally likely?
Is n always divisible by k?
May the input array be shuffled in place?
How should randomness be supplied for testing?
hints: A uniformly random permutation cut into consecutive blocks gives a uniformly random equal-size division.
Fisher-Yates produces each permutation with equal probability when each swap index is uniform.
Copy nums, swap position i with r mod (i + 1) for i from n - 1 down to 1, then slice the copy into k blocks of n / k.
invariants: positions above i are final after step i
the multiset of elements never changes
tradeoffs: Injected random values make tests deterministic; a real implementation would draw them from a generator
hack2hire:68ac67eb1bf7d2097f647efe.variantLabel: Single variant: reproducible random split into k equal groups

clarifyingQuestions: Is the condition about the k largest items or about consecutive items?
What if n < k from the start?
Are removed items always the most expensive ones?
hints: Any k items fit the threshold exactly when the k most expensive remaining items do.
Removing a cheaper item never helps more than removing the most expensive one.
Sort ascending and keep the sum of the window of the k largest remaining; drop the top item and slide the window until the sum is small enough or fewer than k remain.
invariants: after r removals the remaining items are the n - r cheapest
the window sum equals the sum of the k largest remaining prices
chooseWhen: Threshold checks over the largest k elements
tradeoffs: Sorting dominates; a heap gives the same result with more bookkeeping
hack2hire:6770783f366afdc1233e4ff8.variantLabel: Single variant: fewest removals so any k items fit the threshold

clarifyingQuestions: How is a report identified for removal?
What does a query return when no report covers the point?
Is the average a float or rounded?
Are coordinates integers?
hints: A point query of a range update is a prefix sum over a difference array.
Keep two difference arrays: one for speed sums and one for report counts.
Use Fenwick trees for the difference arrays: add at start, subtract at end; the average at p is prefix-sum(p) / prefix-count(p), and a hash map of live copies decides removals.
invariants: the prefix sums at p equal the totals over live reports covering p
a removal only touches the trees when a live copy exists
tradeoffs: Fenwick trees need bounded integer coordinates; a dynamic segment tree handles larger ranges at a higher constant
hack2hire:69c1e01c21f6ab4226964e08.variantLabel: Single variant: average reported speed at a point with add and remove

clarifyingQuestions: What exactly is returned: walking distance, number of scooters or time?
May you switch scooters when riding past another one?
Can scooters stand at or past finish?
hints: Switching to a scooter you pass never hurts, because the new one reaches at least as far.
Then every unit within 10 to the right of a scooter is ridden.
Sort the positions below finish, sweep the union of the ride segments clipped to finish, and subtract its length from finish.
invariants: the covered length never exceeds finish
segments are processed in increasing start order
chooseWhen: Coverage of a line by fixed-length intervals
tradeoffs: Sorting gives O(m log m) independent of finish; unit simulation is O(finish)
hack2hire:6a7fdd1bd713d873ca7adf14.variantLabel: Single variant: least walking with 10-unit scooters

constraints: variables are runs of lowercase letters
parentheses are balanced and never empty
clarifyingQuestions: Should like terms be combined (a+a -> 2a)?
Can the expression start with a unary minus?
How is a negative first term written?
Are variable names single letters?
hints: A minus in front of a parenthesis flips the sign of every term inside it.
Track the sign that applies to the current parenthesis level on a stack.
Scan once: on "(" push current_group_sign * pending_sign, on ")" pop, and emit each variable with group_sign * pending_sign; then join with the first term unsigned when positive.
invariants: the stack top is the sign applied to the current group
terms keep their left-to-right order
tradeoffs: A sign stack avoids recursion depth limits; a recursive parser is clearer but recursion grows with nesting
hack2hire:677b092f78175fce2ecdfc0e.variantLabel: Single variant: drop parentheses and push signs onto the variables

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
clarifyingQuestions: Is s guaranteed to be a palindrome?
Is the comparison plain alphabetical order?
hints: A palindrome is determined by its left half and its middle character.
Because s is a palindrome, at most one letter has an odd count, and it must be the middle.
Build the left half from count // 2 copies of each letter in order a to z, add the odd letter, then append the reversed left half.
invariants: the result has the same letter counts as s
the left half is sorted
tradeoffs: Counting sort is linear; sorting the half is O(n log n) and equally correct

clarifyingQuestions: How much snow melts per day, and is it applied before or after the new snow?
What is asked: ascent, steepest step or passable days?
Does melting depend on elevation?
Is the answer per day or only after the last day?
hints: Simulate the snow depth at each point day by day; it never goes below zero.
The ascent only counts upward steps between neighbours.
Keep one array of accumulated snow; each day add the snowfall, subtract min(melt, depth), then sum max(0, h[i+1] - h[i]).
invariants: snow depth is never negative
each day uses only the previous day's depths
tradeoffs: Incremental state is linear per day; replaying history is quadratic in the number of days
hack2hire:68f29e6ef567e950995157ea.variantLabel: Single variant: total climb along the trail after each day

constraints: stock names are 1 to 10 uppercase letters
the total length of all returned rankings is at most 2e6
clarifyingQuestions: How are ties between equal totals ordered?
Does the ranking include every stock or the top k?
Can quantities be negative (sells)?
hints: Store the running total per stock in a hash map.
Rankings requested back to back without new trades are identical, so cache the sorted list.
Mark the cache dirty on every trade; on a ranking request re-sort by (-total, name) only when dirty, and return a copy so callers cannot change the cache.
invariants: the cache is valid exactly when no trade happened since it was built
the map holds the sum of all recorded quantities per stock
tradeoffs: Caching makes repeated rankings a copy; incremental re-positioning would also speed alternating workloads
hack2hire:68dc6c86dd5418be11109b14.variantLabel: Single variant: rank stocks by total traded quantity with caching

constraints: keys are 1 to 20 lowercase letters, distinct
clarifyingQuestions: Are ids or keys returned?
What happens at a position where no key matches?
Can a key contain ":"?
Are keys unique?
hints: Greedy longest match only needs, at each position, the longest key that starts there.
A trie lets you test every key prefix of the remaining text in one walk.
Walk the trie from the current index, recording the last node that ends a key; emit its id and jump past it, or emit the character and advance by one.
invariants: every output consumes at least one character
the walk never goes deeper than the longest key
tradeoffs: A trie bounds work by the longest key; testing every key is simpler but O(n * dictionary size)

clarifyingQuestions: Can windowSize exceed n?
Which start wins a tie?
Is the target the value or the index?
hints: The count changes by at most one per element as the window slides.
Only update the answer on a strictly larger count to keep the smallest start.
Count the first window, then for each next start subtract nums[i - 1] == target and add nums[i + windowSize - 1] == target.
invariants: the running count equals the target occurrences in the current window
best start is the first window reaching the best count
tradeoffs: Sliding counts are linear; prefix sums are equally fast with O(n) extra space
hack2hire:68ac3bd61bf7d2097f647eec.variantLabel: Single variant: earliest window with the most copies of a value

clarifyingQuestions: Can query indices repeat?
Are indices 0-based?
Can query be empty?
hints: Suffix maxima can be computed from right to left.
When a new larger value appears the count restarts at 1; an equal value increments it.
Precompute count[i] for every i in one backward pass, then answer each query by lookup.
invariants: best and count describe nums[i:] after processing i
counts are at least 1
chooseWhen: Many suffix queries over a static array
tradeoffs: Precomputation costs O(n) memory but answers each query in O(1)
hack2hire:6a51443a665efda9311f60c6.variantLabel: Single variant: count of the suffix maximum per query

constraints: processId and threadId are 1 to 8 letters or digits
timestamps are integers 0 to 1e9 without leading zeros
content is 0 to 30 printable ASCII characters and may contain ":"
clarifyingQuestions: What is the task: grouping, ordering or summarising?
Can the content contain colons?
How are equal timestamps ordered?
Are timestamps compared as numbers?
hints: Split each entry only at its first three colons; the content may contain more.
Timestamps must be compared as integers, not strings.
Stable-sort by the key (processId, threadId, timestamp) and output the original strings.
invariants: the output is a permutation of the input
equal keys keep input order
tradeoffs: A stable sort keeps ties deterministic; bucketing first is equivalent but uses more structures
hack2hire:69ab8d9d4b133b6a8f3a699f.variantLabel: Inferred variant 1: logs ordered by process, thread and time

constraints: processId and threadId are 1 to 8 letters or digits
timestamps are integers 0 to 1e9 without leading zeros
content is 0 to 30 printable ASCII characters and may contain ":"
clarifyingQuestions: Which statistics should each thread report?
Is a thread identified by threadId alone or by (processId, threadId)?
What is the output format?
hints: A thread is identified by its process and thread id together.
Count, minimum and maximum can all be updated in one pass.
Keep [count, min, max] per pair in a hash map, then sort the pairs and format each summary string.
invariants: each summary covers exactly the entries of its pair
first <= last for every pair
tradeoffs: Running aggregates use O(g) memory; storing all timestamps is simpler but O(n)
hack2hire:69ab90f64b133b6a8f3a69a3.variantLabel: Inferred variant 2: per-thread entry count and time range

clarifyingQuestions: Is the comparison average >= threshold or strictly greater?
What if precedingMinutes exceeds the number of minutes?
Is a count or the list of alert minutes returned?
hints: Compare sums instead of averages to stay in exact integers.
Each window differs from the previous one by one entering and one leaving value.
Keep a running sum; once i >= k - 1 compare it with alertThreshold * k and count, then subtract numCalls[i - k + 1].
invariants: the running sum equals the current window
no alert is counted before k values are seen
tradeoffs: Integer sum comparison avoids floating-point averages; prefix sums would also work
hack2hire:6a97291f0ca9cc4e1c789d82.variantLabel: Single variant: count of windows whose average reaches the threshold

constraints: teleporters are "from,to" with 1 <= from < lastSquare, 0 <= to <= lastSquare, to != from, from unique
clarifyingQuestions: Is the output sorted and deduplicated?
Does a teleporter destination with its own teleporter chain?
Is lastSquare reachable by overshooting?
hints: Each roll yields exactly one end square.
Overshooting the board ends the turn on lastSquare without teleporting.
Parse "from,to" into a map, compute min(lastSquare, landing) or the teleport target per roll, and return the sorted distinct set.
invariants: at most dieSides distinct answers
every answer is between 0 and lastSquare
chooseWhen: One-step transitions of a board game
tradeoffs: A set plus sort is simple; a boolean array over squares avoids sorting for dense outputs
hack2hire:68c9aaf3212d48d6e0f5977c.variantLabel: Inferred variant 1: end squares of one turn

constraints: teleporters are "from,to" with 1 <= from < lastSquare, 0 <= to <= lastSquare, to != from, from unique
clarifyingQuestions: Can the player choose the roll, or is the minimum over all possible rolls?
What is returned when the last square cannot be reached?
Does the game start on square 0?
hints: Treat squares as graph nodes and turns as unweighted edges.
Squares that hold a teleporter are never the end of a turn, but their destinations are.
Run a breadth-first search from 0 with the turn rule as the successor function and stop when lastSquare is dequeued or discovered.
invariants: each square is enqueued at most once
the distance of a square is the fewest turns that end on it
chooseWhen: Shortest paths with unit edge costs
tradeoffs: BFS is linear in edges; dynamic relaxation is simpler but may repeat passes
hack2hire:68c9ac13212d48d6e0f5977d.variantLabel: Inferred variant 2: fewest turns to reach the last square

constraints: release is only called for a running job
clarifyingQuestions: May a job join running jobs of its type while others wait?
Which waiting jobs are admitted when the lock becomes free?
How are blocked threads woken without busy-waiting?
Can the same job id be reused?
hints: The lock state is just the running type and how many jobs of it are running.
To avoid starvation, a new job must not overtake jobs already waiting.
Keep a FIFO queue; acquire admits only when the queue is empty and the running type matches or nothing runs; when the last running job releases, admit the queue prefix with the head job's type.
invariants: running jobs always share one type
a waiting queue implies at least one running job
chooseWhen: Group mutual exclusion between job classes
tradeoffs: FIFO admission prevents starvation at some throughput cost; letting same-type jobs join freely can starve the other type
hack2hire:6a4d6a5560d5cca82da2fe23.variantLabel: Single variant: two-type reader-style lock with FIFO admission

constraints: url characters are letters, digits and "/:.~-=&?"
clarifyingQuestions: What does a key without "=" map to?
How are repeated keys represented?
Is percent-encoding decoded?
Are empty pairs ignored?
hints: Only the first "?" separates the path from the query; later "?" belong to values.
Split each pair at its first "=", so values may contain "=".
Collect values per key in order; at the end map single values to strings and repeated ones to lists.
invariants: each non-empty piece with a non-empty key contributes exactly one value
list values keep the query order
tradeoffs: Manual splitting is linear and explicit; a regular expression is shorter but hides the edge rules
hack2hire:68e02ab4846fd9cdeb438e4e.variantLabel: Single variant: query string to key-value mapping
